0.0.n: さん adds politeness when addressing the whole audience.

0.2.n: A standard daytime greeting; the final は is pronounced わ.

1.0.n: Part of the organization name ひらがなネット; hiragana is also a Japanese writing system.

1.1.n: This completes the organization name ひらがなネット, rather than referring independently to the internet.

1.2.n: Marks the organization where she teaches.

1.3.n: Describes the type of cooking in 和食料理.

1.4.n: Combines with 和食 to specify what she teaches.

1.5.n: Marks 和食料理 as what she teaches.

1.6.n: て-form of 教える + いる describes her ongoing teaching work and modifies あきこ.

1.7.n: This is the speaker’s given name.

1.8.n: Politely ends her self-introduction; the subject I is understood.

2.0.n: Refers to the current cooking lesson.

2.1.n: Marks 今回 as the topic: what they will do this time.

2.3.n: Refers to chicken meat here, rather than a live bird.

2.4.n: Links chicken to 照り焼き, identifying the main ingredient.

2.5.n: Names a dish or cooking style with a glossy, typically sweet soy-based glaze.

2.6.n: Marks 鶏の照り焼き as the dish being made.

2.7.n: Polite form of 作る; here it announces the planned cooking activity.

3.0.n: Signals a transition from the introduction to starting the cooking.

3.2.n: Used with に to describe doing the activity with someone else.

3.3.n: Makes 一緒に describe how they will cook: as a shared activity.

3.4.n: The ましょう form of 作る politely invites the audience to join the activity.

0.tip: 皆さん is a polite, friendly way to address a group.

1.lit: At Hiragana Net, Japanese cuisine cooking teaching Akiko am.
1.tip: 教えている comes before あきこ, describing her as the person who teaches Japanese cooking.

2.lit: This time, as for, chicken’s teriyaki will make.
2.tip: 作ります can describe a future plan; Japanese does not need a separate future-tense form.

3.lit: Well then, together let’s make it.
3.tip: Changing 作ります to 作りましょう turns an announcement into a polite invitation.
